about.title: Huntington Park Medical Malpractice Claims
about.longDescription: Huntington Park residents rely on nearby clinics, urgent care centers, and Los Angeles County hospitals for everything from routine visits to emergency care. Most of the time, that care goes as expected. But when a diagnosis is missed, a surgery goes wrong, or medication errors cause harm, patients and families are often left confused about what happened and what comes next. Medical malpractice cases in California are governed by MICRA, a law that limits certain damages and imposes short deadlines for filing a claim. Because these cases almost always require a qualified medical expert to explain how the care fell short of an accepted standard, they can be more complex than other injury claims. LawProactive doesn't practice law or evaluate your medical records. Instead, we connect Huntington Park residents with an independent attorney who can review the details, explain your options, and help you understand whether your situation may qualify for a claim.

whyChoose.title: Why Talk to an Attorney Early

items.title: Strict, Short Deadlines
items.desc: California generally requires malpractice claims within one year of discovering the harm, and never more than three years from the injury itself. Waiting too long can close the door on a claim entirely, regardless of its merits.

items.title: 90-Day Notice Requirement
items.desc: Before filing suit, California law generally requires sending the healthcare provider a 90-day notice of intent to sue. An attorney can help make sure this step is handled correctly and on time.

items.title: Expert Review Is Usually Required
items.desc: Because a bad medical outcome alone doesn't prove malpractice, a qualified medical expert typically must confirm that the care fell below an accepted standard. An experienced attorney knows how to arrange for that kind of review.

items.question: I had a bad outcome after treatment in Huntington Park — does that mean it was malpractice?
items.answer: Not necessarily. California law recognizes that medicine involves risk, and a poor result by itself isn't proof of malpractice. An attorney would need to review whether the care provided fell below the accepted medical standard, usually with input from a qualified medical expert.

items.question: How much time do I have to bring a claim?
items.answer: Under California's MICRA rules, claims generally must be brought within one year of discovering the injury, and no later than three years from when it occurred. There's also a required 90-day notice period before filing suit, so it's best to speak with an attorney as soon as you suspect something went wrong.

items.question: Are damages limited in California malpractice cases?
items.answer: Yes, MICRA sets a cap on non-economic damages, though that cap has been set to rise annually. Economic damages, like medical bills and lost income, are generally not subject to the same cap. An independent attorney can explain how this may apply to your specific circumstances.
